questions.q: What do integration-and-scale objections more often test, compared to data-and-security objections?
options: Whether the candidate memorized Salesforce's full list of governor limits
Whether a specific design number or choice holds up as volumes get bigger, change shape, or arrive faster than assumed
Whether the candidate can draw a diagram without any preparation
Whether the candidate agrees with every panelist's opinion
questions.explain: This domain's objections tend to probe whether a chosen threshold, interval, or approach was actually reasoned through against realistic scale and timing pressure, not guessed.

questions.q: In the Carrow Equipment real-time-vs-batch objection, why does the model answer defend real-time integration despite its added complexity?
options: Because real-time integration is always simpler than batch in every case
Because batch integration is against Salesforce's platform terms of service

Because a fifteen-minute-old inventory number creates exactly the staleness risk the scenario calls out as a real fulfillment problem, and the added complexity is the accepted cost of avoiding that specific, named risk
Because the panel always prefers whichever option is more technically complex
questions.explain: The answer restates the specific business consequence (stale inventory causing a fulfillment problem) that was already reasoned through in the original design, rather than defending complexity for its own sake.

questions.q: What makes the model answer to the Nimbus Mobile scale-assumption objection ("what if actual volume is triple what you assumed") strong?
options: It insists the original volume assumption was definitely correct and refuses to engage further
It admits the entire tiered storage design would need to be scrapped
It avoids answering by saying scale questions are out of scope
It shows the design degrades gracefully by tuning the live-query/archive threshold rather than requiring a full redesign if the assumption is wrong
questions.explain: A strong answer names the assumption's consequence and shows the design has a known, proportionate response (tuning a threshold) rather than breaking entirely if the assumption turns out wrong.

questions.q: What distinguishes a strong failure-path answer (for example, Alder Trust Bank's KYC vendor call failing) from a weak one?
options: A strong answer names the specific failure mode and a scenario-appropriate response (routing to manual review rather than defaulting to approval or blocking indefinitely), treating failure handling as a first-class design decision
A strong answer claims the integration will never fail under any circumstances
A weak answer always includes more technical detail than a strong one
A strong answer defers the entire question to the panel to answer instead
questions.explain: Treating the failure path as an afterthought ("we'd add error handling") is the weak pattern this lesson warns against; naming the specific failure mode and response is the strong one.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what are objections in the integration-and-scale domain usually actually testing?
options: Whether the candidate chose the one single "correct" number in every case
Whether the candidate can recite exact governor limit figures from memory
Whether there is real reasoning behind a chosen number or threshold that can flex when the underlying premise changes
Whether the candidate's design uses the newest Salesforce product by name
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that these objections rarely hinge on whether a specific number was 'right' — they test whether real reasoning backs it and whether that reasoning holds up if the premise shifts.
